This study investigates how jet fires respond to acoustic excitation in a linearized, turbulent environment. Employing a purely numerical approach, the simulation framework incorporates an active flame method within both the gas and energy equations of Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) models. This method simulates a standing acoustic wave along the jet's centerline to linearly test the turbulence model's capacity to describe flame behavior under acoustic excitation. Validation against a linearized RANS model of a turbulent premixed jet flame excited by a downstream cross-flow speaker confirms that the active flame method effectively replicates a premixed jet flame oscillating via acoustic excitation. Furthermore, the framework was applied to a fire excited by a speaker, demonstrating its ability to linearly model this scenario. Results indicate that the oscillation frequency of the induced flame rings aligns with the driver's output frequency, while the amplitude correlates with the driver's voltage. Additionally, the findings reveal that the turbulent flame coherence increases with rising excitation amplitude. Ultimately, this research provides a numerical framework capable of linearly simulating the oscillation of a turbulent jet fire driven by acoustic excitation. Nonlocal gravity models offer potential solutions to issues in both general relativity and the observation of gravitational waves. This article introduces a constitutive approach to nonlocal gravitation, drawing parallels with nonlocal elasticity from continuum mechanics. Within this framework, the constitutive matrix is defined by a background theory—potentially general relativity or another nonlocal variant—distinct from the active metric that determines gravitational interactions. We examine the implications of this distinction for wave propagation and provide a constitutive model aligned with recent nonlocal observations. The formulation ensures that gravitational wave speeds depend on wave amplitude and frequency through a dielectric-like tensor, while maintaining special relativistic speeds for plane waves in vacuum. Additionally, we derive a modified Einstein-Ainstein field equation that accounts for nonlocal effects.

We analyze the variable-time intervals between transient outbursts from X-ray binaries in the Milky Way's central region. For systems with measured orbital periods, we establish a connection between these intervals and the accretion flow's mean residence time within the system's orbit. Leveraging this relationship, we examine the likely states of the gas supplying dormant binaries in the Galactic Centre. Specifically, we scrutinize the claim of commutable time variability in X-ray transients from the GC as evidence for general variability in the supply of gas from the Galactic disc to the central supermassive black hole. We find that for known systems with orbital periods exceeding a few hours—where the mean residence time is long enough to generate observable gaps between outbursts—the accreting white dwarfs or neutron stars likely operate as dormant systems with atmospheres or as very low mass X-ray binaries with atmospheres. Conversely, for putative systems with shorter periods (approximately < 3 hours) from the GC, the presence of long time-dependent variability implies that the companion star's mean residence time, and consequently its physical size, must be exceptionally large, possibly originating directly from a molecular cloud. Such a system would represent a unique example of a "super-donor" in the GC. However, we note that no candidate with a period shorter than a few hours has been confirmed to date. Finally, we argue that the observed long-term variability in outburst intervals for the GX 3-1 system is most plausibly due to random fluctuations in the accretion rate onto its neutron star, rather than genuine long-term temporal variability in the supply of gas from the Galactic disc to the central black hole.

Bipartite vertex splitting, a operation where a vertex is removed and reattached to new nodes, serves as the reverse of the well-known blow-up operation. This paper introduces a method to limit the number of FPT algorithms required for deciding whether a graph can be made bipartite through at most $k$ vertex splits. Additionally, we integrate this approach with a standard topological minor decomposition tree. As an example, we apply these methods to determine if a graph is 3-colorable via at most $k$ bipartite vertex splittings, relying on the fact that tripartite graphs are 3-colorable. Our method demonstrates that this decision problem is solvable in $O(3^{w(G)}\cdot poly(k))$ time, where $w(G)$ represents the size of the maximum edge weight in $G$ (with edge weights defined by the count of connecting vertices in $K_3$ subgraphs). Consequently, the problem is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to $k$. We also establish several other results concerning bipartite vertex splitting. Notably, we prove that for any integer $r\ge 1$, deciding if a graph becomes $r$-colorable through at most $k$ bipartite vertex splits is equivalent to determining whether a graph's clique of size $r+1$ can be formed from its subunits using at most $k$ topological minor operations. Finally, we provide the explicit form of the tame function associated with this problem. (Our method of incorporating the parameter $r$ differs from a recent approach by Fomin, Grandoni, and Krupka [SODA 2025], which utilizes a distinct parameterization). High-frequency low-and-critical frequency CPU side-channel attacks have historically been constrained by feasible attack durations. We introduce HyperDegrade, a novel side-channel attack framework that utilizes high-frequency CPU traces to construct low-frequency traces through simulation, extending attack possibilities beyond the limits of real-time access. We evaluate this approach on an Intel Xeon E5-2690 v4 processor, demonstrating an attack reconstructing a 128-bit AES key in approximately 10 hours using a 3.5 GHz trace to emulate a 1.1 GHz frequency. Furthermore, we assess HyperDegrade on other CPU configurations, showcasing adaptability across different architectures and confirming that the attack efficacy scales with the ratio between access and target frequencies. These findings highlight that high-frequency leaks, when combined with simulation, can compromise any low-frequency implementation. To mitigate these risks, we offer practical countermeasures and provide a detailed efficacy analysis. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/SHIVAM-109/HyperDegrade.

This paper introduces a table tennis game modeled as a sequential game of imperfect information to examine how conventional networks of multi-agent systems (MAS) play games with imperfect information. The proposed tactical multi-agent system comprises two MAS teams, each containing two agents with limited computational resources. The agent with higher computational limits serves as the receiver, while the agent with lower limits acts as the server. The tactical MAS for the receiving team (R-MAT) utilizes limited detectable information to select an optimal saving strategy against the opposing tactical MAS (S-MAT). Operating on a simple star-shaped topological structure, the R-MAT communicates with the server agent (S-A) through an intermediate agent (I-A). Similarly, the R-MAT's agents (IA-A and IA-B) exchange detection information about the service action via the I-A before deciding on the best saving action. Leveraging the Shapley value from cooperative game theory, this system maximizes the collective Shapley value of its constituent agents. These findings indicate that the Shapley value-based tactical MAS effectively leverages limited detectable and computational resources to exceed the capabilities of teams utilizing advanced AI. Machines playing pedagogical roles have significant potential for automatically scaling up educational systems. To harness this potential, systems must accurately identify student knowledge gaps and select appropriate instructions to address them. Consequently, pedagogical agents require a knowledge acquisition (KA) framework to explicitly gain and apply domain knowledge through structured interactions. Within this framework, students act as pupils providing input, while humans or other systems serve as instructors who set goals, define the knowledge structure, evaluate statements, and offer feedback. Although human-in-the-loop KA has been extensively researched for decades, automated approaches are now feasible due to substantial advances in natural language processing techniques and resources. This paper reviews existing KA methods, beginning with a taxonomy of common approaches and subsequently examining recent methods for goal setting, structure definition, statement evaluation, and feedback generation. Furthermore, the review analyzes recent systems integrating these methods into comprehensive KA architectures, discusses critical open issues, and outlines potential future research directions. Finally, we consider the feasibility of transitioning from instructor-centered to student-centered conversations to resolve current challenges and ultimately achieve fully automatic KA. Such an transition could unlock numerous benefits, including improved efficiency in refining large language models, easier incorporation of expert knowledge into artificial intelligence systems, and simplified updates to educational agents when curricula change. However, these benefits rely on successful research efforts to enable fully automatic KA. Such efforts must follow a structured process covering recent evaluated methods, real-world KA scenarios, successful industry deployments, and identified research gaps. Guided by this framework, the community can prioritize solutions for fully automatic KA, whether through advanced NLP techniques, neural architecture search, meta-learning, or multi-task learning approaches.

At colliders, neutral particles are identified either through their decay into displaced vertices or via missing energy. Distinguishing between these detection methods for new physics candidates is challenging, as it relies on the mass and decay length of the particle. We examine the optimal strategy for searching for light sterile neutrinos and axion-like particles (ALPs) arising from meson decays at Belle II. While looking for two-body decays in missing energy is generally more sensitive for ALPs, this approach is limited by statistics for masses exceeding 100 MeV. For sub-100 MeV ALPs, the sensitivity to invisible $B$ decays could reach $\mathcal{O}(10^{-6})$, potentially surpassing the sensitivity to displaced vertices by a factor of two to four. Conversely, for light sterile neutrinos with masses around 100 MeV, the limit on invisible $B$ decays at Belle II is likely weaker than that on displaced vertices; however, the sensitivity to sterile neutrinos could improve by an order of magnitude beyond current sensitivities at fixed-target experiments.

Hypothesis testing in statistics typically relies on two main approaches: p-values and Bayes factors. While Bayes factors offer the advantage of providing a direct measure of evidence for both the null and alternative hypotheses, their practical application has been limited because generating the necessary data for calculation is computationally demanding. This paper re-examines the use of Bayes factors, introducing methods to exploit their non-linear characteristics and introducing a novel regression-based technique for producing reliable estimates from low-precision calculations. We evaluate these methods using simulated datasets and a real-world analysis of the "dunning crisis," comparing the effectiveness of different strategies for utilizing Bayes factors. Our results indicate that combining low-cost computations with regression-based estimation yields the most efficient approach for datasets exceeding a few thousand in size. Furthermore, we observe that multiple testing corrections substantially reduce the evidence required to conclude that an effect is real, a finding that could help shift focus back toward the scientific value of Bayes factors. Finally, we present a streamlined method for calculating prior predictive probabilities to assess model fit, completing a comprehensive workflow for efficiently applying Bayes factors in hypothesis testing. This workflow is implemented via an R package named `tf-bf`.

Discourse indicators are lexical items used to establish and track referents of superlexical constructs, such as discursive and anaphoric expressions. Given their reference-oriented nature, discourse indicators are a ideal focus for named entity recognition techniques. However, existing methods often fail to capture the nuance of different indicator types. For instance, anaphoric indicators like "this," "that," "such," and "the above" are treated identically by current algorithms, despite carrying distinct meanings. Similarly, discursive indicators are categorized into just two groups: anaphoric and topicalizing. We introduce DiscSense, an unsupervised approach for pluralizing categories of discourse indicators by deriving a set of meaningful types from the data itself. This method combines lexical statistics, heuristics, and a type-building algorithm. Applied to two English corpora, DiscSense successfully created a hierarchy of semantically different types for both anaphoric and discursive indicators. As a byproduct, the algorithm yields a simple lexical density score for each type, revealing that anaphoric indicators are generally more dense than discursive ones. Experimental results show that our type classifications align well with human judgments. Additionally, a basic classification model utilizing our types outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on a standard dataset for classifying anaphoric discursive indicators. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the derived types and their associated lexical items. Our types offer a precise characterization of anaphoric indicators, facilitating the training of targeted neural networks for detection tasks. Furthermore, the categories satisfy MUC criteria for meaningfulness, granularity, and structural coherence. We anticipate that this detailed classification will be valuable for various linguistic investigations. The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/abhishek-sharma29/DiscSense. Keywords: anaphora, discourse, lexical density, named entity recognition, unsupervised learning.

Regular expression inequalities appear frequently in wildcode and are commonly addressed by automata-based techniques. However, these methods struggle with DNF-catastrophe phenomena and suffer from poor scalability as expression complexity increases. This paper introduces a term rewriting system capable of resolving both equality and inequality constraints over extended regular expressions that include intersection and complement operators. The approach combines co-inductive reasoning with inductive reasoning to manage these operators effectively. Additionally, the system incorporates a simplification rule for inequalities that bypasses standard rewriting processes. Extensive testing conducted on a dataset of real-world regular expression inequalities from source code, performed between November 2020 and October 2021, demonstrates that this framework successfully tackles a broader range of challenges than existing automata-based systems. The implemented system is accessible at https://github.com/verifafse/ERT. These findings highlight the potential of term rewriting systems to address verification problems in extended regular expressions, an area where such applications have previously been limited.

Detecting local magnetic field fluctuations represents a significant challenge in magnetometry. In this study, we introduce an interferometric approach to observe minute magnetic variations induced by a bulk superconductor through a vacuum atomic fountain. With the atomic waveform, we directly image the expulsion of the local magnetic field caused by the Meissner effect in the superconductor, enabling a sensing sensitivity of approximately 20 fT per run at a 600 s integration time. This sensitivity exceeds that of a comparable magnetometer operating in the absence of the superconductor by a factor of ten. This enhancement is achieved by shifting the operation point near the center of the Rabi oscillation, where atoms exhibit heightened sensitivity to magnetic fields. To implement this, we generated Rabi oscillations using a radio-frequency (RF) pulse, creating a "Rabi magnetometer" configuration. We anticipate that this observation technique will function as a valuable analytical tool for examining the local magnetic field fluctuations of various superconducting materials.
